notes.meaning: God tells the people to search the streets and public squares of Jerusalem for even one person who acts with justice and seeks the truth. If a single honest person could be found, the Lord promises to spare the entire city. This shows how ready God is to forgive, yet moral rot had spread through the whole community.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic translations, following the Latin Vulgate, translate the search as seeking 'faith' rather than 'truth'.

notes.meaning: The people often use solemn religious language, swearing 'As surely as the Lord lives.' Yet their oaths are completely false, because their hearts are far from God. Using the Lord's holy name to cover up dishonesty only adds to their guilt.

Jeremiah reminds the Lord that His eyes look for genuine honesty, not empty religious words. God had already sent painful hardships to correct the people, but they refused to learn from His discipline. They hardened their faces like flint and stubbornly refused to turn back to Him.

Jeremiah first wonders if this foolish and wicked behavior belongs only to the poor. He reasons that ordinary laborers had little chance for formal instruction in God's law. He hopes that their sin is simply the result of ignorance.

The prophet decides to take his message to the educated and wealthy leaders of the land. He expects them to know God's law and live by it. Instead, he finds that the ruling classes are even more corrupt, having deliberately torn off God's yoke to live however they please.

Because their rebellions are so great, deadly danger will fall on the people like wild beasts. The lion, wolf, and leopard picture fierce, ravenous invaders—the Babylonian army—who will trap the citizens inside their towns. Anyone who dares to step outside will be torn to pieces.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters understand the wild beasts as general figures of desolating calamities rather than specific invading empires.

notes.meaning: God asks how He can possibly overlook such brazen sin. His people have abandoned Him to worship and swear by powerless idols. Even though the Lord provided food and wealth in abundance, they used their strength to commit adultery and crowded into houses of prostitution.

The people are compared to well-fed, lustful horses roaming about with unbridled desire. Each person shamelessly covets his neighbor's wife. Their material blessings only fueled their selfish appetites instead of drawing them to God.
The Lord asks whether He can let such blatant wrongdoing go unpunished. Because He is the righteous Judge of all the earth, His holy nature demands that a nation so wicked face a reckoning.

God directs the foreign invaders to march up to Jerusalem and strip away her branches like an overgrown vineyard. He will not destroy the nation entirely, but will prune away the ungodly who do not truly belong to Him. This judgment leaves a remnant behind for future renewal.

Both the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah have acted with total treachery toward the Lord. They broke the sacred covenant agreement just like an unfaithful spouse, leaving God fully justified in bringing judgment.

The people lied about the Lord by convincing themselves that He would never actually step in to punish them. They assumed they were completely safe and that neither war nor famine would ever reach their homes. They lived in practical unbelief, ignoring God's direct warnings.

The crowd dismissed the true prophets as empty windbags whose words held no real substance. They claimed that the Spirit of God did not speak through them, and they arrogantly wished that the threatened disasters would fall on the prophets instead.

Because the mockers called His warnings empty wind, the Lord declares that His message in Jeremiah's mouth will become a consuming fire. The rebellious people will be like dry wood. The fiery judgment of God's word will bring about their swift downfall.

God warns Judah that He is bringing an ancient, powerful nation from far away to wage war against them. This Babylonian foe speaks a foreign language that the Jews do not understand. Because of this language barrier, there will be no way to plead for mercy or negotiate peace.

The invading soldiers are mighty fighters whose arrow quivers are compared to open graves. Their archers shoot with such deadly accuracy that every flying arrow brings certain death to someone on the battlefield.

The invaders will plunder the land completely, eating the grain and food meant for the people's children. They will take away the herds, strip the vineyards and fig trees, and tear down the fortified cities in which the people wrongly placed their confidence.

Even during this terrible destruction, the Lord promises that He will not wipe out His people completely. In His covenant mercy, He sets a clear boundary on how far the enemy can go, sparing a surviving remnant.

When the people ask why God has brought these harsh afflictions on them, Jeremiah must give them a direct answer. Because they abandoned the Lord and served foreign gods in their own homeland, they will now be forced to serve foreign rulers in a land that is not theirs.

Jeremiah is commanded to announce this message publicly to the house of Jacob and declare it throughout Judah. God ensures that every family in the covenant community hears the charges and understands what is coming.

The Lord addresses the people as foolish and lacking all spiritual understanding. They have working physical eyes and ears, yet they stubbornly refuse to see God's works or listen to His truth. Their deliberate sin has made them as spiritually lifeless as the idols they worship.

God asks why the people do not tremble before Him, seeing that He places shifting sand as an enduring boundary for the wild sea. Even though giant waves toss and roar, they cannot cross over the line He established. The raging ocean obeys its Creator, but God's own people refuse to listen.
Unlike the ocean that stays within its borders, God's people have stubborn, rebellious hearts. They have deliberately turned their backs on their Lord and wandered far away into sin.

The people never stop to consider that they should revere the Lord who kindly supplies their daily bread. He regularly sends the autumn rains to help the seeds grow and the spring rains to ripen the crops, preserving the scheduled weeks for a fruitful harvest.

differ.view: Some understand the 'latter rain' spiritually as special seasons of grace and church revival that prepare believers for heaven.

notes.meaning: The persistent sins of the nation are what turned these natural blessings away. God stood ready to give His bounty, but their rebellion created a barrier that cut off the needed rains and good harvests.
Cruel and predatory men are found living right inside the covenant community. Like bird-catchers hiding in ambush with traps, these wicked individuals scheme to ruin and exploit innocent neighbors.

Just as a hunter's cage becomes stuffed with captured birds, so the homes of these corrupt men are packed with dishonest gains. By cheating the vulnerable, they have climbed to high status and built vast fortunes.

The dishonest leaders have grown fat, sleek, and comfortable through their greedy lifestyles, surpassing even pagan nations in wickedness. They refuse to defend the legal rights of orphans or give justice to the poor, yet they continue to enjoy worldly success.
The Lord repeats His solemn warning, asking if He can leave such terrible injustice unaddressed. Because He is a holy and just God, He must inevitably step in to punish such an unrepentant nation.

God points out an astonishing and horrifying situation taking place in the land. The spiritual and moral decline of His chosen nation is so shocking that it should cause everyone to recoil with dread.

The prophets preach comforting lies, the priests abuse their power by collaborating with those lies, and the common people gladly accept the deception so they can remain in their sins. God leaves them with a piercing question: what will they do when His judgment finally falls and everything collapses?
